items.title: Is this OMI, subendocardial ischemia, LVH, or some combination?
items.summary: An ECG the AI model read as anything but occlusion, and a troponin that said otherwise.
items.note: Nossen walks an elderly nursing-home patient with an irregular rhythm and varying P-wave morphology, where the automated model scored subendocardial ischaemia at 66 percent and LVH at 68 percent and never flagged OMI — then the troponin climbed. The multifocal atrial tachycardia differential is the kind of thing that arrives at triage looking like noise. Worth reading alongside the Queen of Hearts cases already in the feed, because this one is the model being confidently wrong.

items.title: Increasing ST elevation. MI ruled out. Must be pericarditis, right?
items.summary: A 30-year-old with chest pain, serial ECGs that keep changing, and no clean answer at the end.
items.note: Frick presents the case and Grauer's commentary refuses to land on either acute pericarditis or OMI from the serial tracings, pinning much of the apparent evolution on heart-rate variability and inconsistent precordial lead placement. That second point is the practical one: the lead-placement artefact he describes is produced by whoever runs the repeat ECG, which on a night shift is often you. It ends on a recommendation for cardiac MRI rather than a diagnosis, which is the honest version.

items.title: The new Footscray Hospital still isn't fully operational or staffed
items.summary: A brand-new Victorian hospital with beds it cannot open, and ACEM saying so on the record.
items.note: ACEM's Mark Putland puts it plainly — if there's no staff to staff them, you've effectively got no beds — which is the distinction between a ribbon-cutting and actual ED capacity. Health Minister Ingrid Stitt's answer is a gradual increase in open beds, meaning the ramping pressure stays distributed across everyone else's department in the meantime. This is his own college commenting on the system he works inside, a week after the statewide doctors' stoppage.

items.title: WHO Pandemic Hub sets goal of detecting outbreaks within 24 hours
items.summary: The detection-to-notification window that decides whether an outbreak is containable or not.
items.note: The Berlin Hub is putting a number on the front end of the chain whose outputs he already reads here — the Disease Outbreak News notices on Bundibugyo in the DRC and the Irkutsk lab death both ran days behind the events they described. A 24-hour target is as much a claim about national reporting willingness as about surveillance technology. Useful as the structural frame behind the individual DONs.

items.title: AI is a determinant of population health. Policy isn't keeping up
items.summary: An argument that AI is not a tool health applies but a force acting on health outcomes.
items.note: Ciriello and Backholer's move is to flip the framing: Australian debate treats health as a sector where AI gets deployed, rather than an outcome AI shapes, and they want consequential systems governed as public-interest infrastructure. The sharpest supporting detail in Croakey's related reporting is that the Office of AI in PM&C does not mention health at all. Relevant to him twice over — it is the policy layer above the clinical AI tools, and his feed already follows the capability releases.

items.title: Mutimer Is Coming to New York & Los Angeles
items.summary: The LA pop-up opens this week and the new collection goes online on the 24th.
items.note: Straight from the brand rather than the trade coverage, which matters because the dates are the point: West Hollywood runs 17–19 October, and Canary on the Frontier is pop-up-exclusive before it hits the site on 24 October. Red Label, the year-round signature range, travels with it. For a label he follows that only opened its first permanent store on Smith Street in March, going to two US cities inside seven months is the interesting part.

items.title: Johnston's knitwear: luxurious and innovative
items.summary: A mill most people know as somebody else's supplier, reviewed on its own label.
items.note: Johnston's of Elgin spins and weaves for half the names in heritage menswear, so a review of what it puts out under its own name is a rare look at a manufacturer judged directly rather than through a brand's markup. Crompton stays on the making and the cloth, which is the end of Permanent Style worth his time, and avoids the bespoke-tailoring register entirely. Provenance-first reading in the same vein as the Beorma leather piece.

items.title: Jalen Ngonda on escaping the sophomore slump
items.summary: The long interview on a Daptone record by an artist already on his shelf.
items.note: Ngonda is in the library, and this is the most substantial sit-down on Doctrine of Love — he describes moving off the Marvin Gaye and Curtis Mayfield register of his debut toward 1950s New Orleans R&B and Chicago and Detroit soul, which is a real shift rather than press-release language. Vince Chiarito and Michael Buckley co-produced. Sits directly next to the Sharon Jones, Thee Sacred Souls and Menahan Street Band end of the collection.

items.title: Hytale adds its first dungeon and a multi-phase boss
items.summary: A survival-crafting game finally shipping hand-built content instead of more systems.
items.note: Out of the Breach lands Hytale's first hand-crafted dungeon with a multi-phase boss fight, plus new items and abilities — the point at which a voxel survival sandbox starts offering designed encounters rather than just tools. That is the same curve Dragonwilds walked with the Scorned Wilderness raid and Kuldra. Massively OP covers survival-game updates more closely than anyone, and this one landed today.

items.title: Melbourne streetwear label Tild has a pop-up all October
items.summary: A month-long shopfront on Gertrude Street, open daily and free to walk into.
items.note: 240 Gertrude Street, 4 October to 1 November, 10am to 4pm daily — a full month rather than the usual long weekend, so it is actually visitable without planning around it. Tild was started in 2021 by Melbourne sisters Tilly and Lucy Comb and runs vintage-inspired cuts under the streetwear surface. Walking distance from Northside Records at 236 Gertrude, which makes one trip do two things.

items.title: This corner wine bar has quietly become an inner north favourite
items.summary: Thirty seats on Nicholson Street, minimal-intervention list, and a courtyard worth the walk.
items.note: Brico took over the old Little Andorra corner at 555 Nicholson Street, started by five friends who met in London, with floor experience out of Embla, Bar Liberty and the Carlton Wine Room — which is why a thirty-seater runs like it does. Simon Ball-Smith's menu is European and built to share: devilled crab on fried green tomato, rock flathead in fig leaves. Northside, low-key, and the sun-dappled courtyard is the reason to go before summer books it out.
